'''Johann Friedrich Pfaff''' (sometimes spelled '''Friederich'''; 22 December 1765 – 21 April 1825) was a German mathematician. He is best known for his work on [[differential equations]] and as [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]]'s doctoral advisor.

==Biography==
Johann Friedrich Pfaff was born 22 December 1765 to Friedrich Burkhard Pfaff (1738-1817) and Mary Magdalena Pfaff (née Brand) in Stuttgart. He was one of seven sons and five daughters.<ref name="dunnington"/>

Pfaff attended the [[Hohe Karlsschule]] from 1774 to 1785, where his classmates included [[Carl Friedrich Kielmeyer]] and {{ill|Ludwig Schubart|de|Ludwig Schubart}}, and where he met his lifelong friend, [[Friedrich Schiller]]. His mathematical talent was noticed early on by his teachers and he came to the attention of [[Charles Eugene, Duke of Württemberg|Duke Charles Eugene]], who sponsored his further studies. In 1785 he went to [[University of Göttingen|Göttingen]], where he studied mathematics under [[Abraham Gotthelf Kästner]] and completed his prize-winning essay on astronomy.{{sfn|Pfaff|1786}} In 1787 he went to [[Berlin]] and studied astronomy under [[Johann Elert Bode|J. E. Bode]];<ref name="dunnington"/><ref name="EB1911">{{Cite EB1911|wstitle=Pfaff, Johann Friedrich|volume=21|pages=339–340}}</ref> there he completed his first notable mathematical work, on [[series (mathematics)|series]] summation.{{sfn|Pfaff|1788a}}  While in Berlin, Pfaff joined [[Christoph Friedrich Nicolai|Friedrich Nicolai]]'s circle of [[Berlin Enlightenment|enlighteners]].<ref name="wussing">{{cite encyclopedia |article=Pfaff, Johann Friedrich |author=Hans Wussing |author-link=Hans Wussing |title=Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography |title-link=Dictionary of Scientific Biography |location=New York |publisher=Charles Scribner's Sons |year=2007}}</ref>

In 1788, on the recommendation of [[Georg Christoph Lichtenberg]], Pfaff became professor of mathematics at the [[University of Helmstedt]]. His [[habilitation|inaugural dissertation]]{{sfn|Pfaff|1788b}} investigates the calculation of [[differential (mathematics)|differentials]].<ref name="dhombres">{{cite book |author=J. Dhombres |author-link=Jean Dhombres |chapter=La méthode fonctionnelle chez J F Pfaff: une filiation Leibnizienne |title=Un parcours en histoire des mathématiques: travaux et recherches |location=Nantes |year=1993 |pages=97-147}}</ref> His subsequent mathematical work at Helmstedt included: nine articles in [[Carl Hindenburg]]'s journals, notably two{{sfn|Pfaff|1795a}}{{sfn|Pfaff|1795b}} linking arithmetic and analysis,<ref>{{cite journal |author=Hans Niels Jahnke |author-link=:de:Hans Niels Jahnke |title=Algebraic analysis in Germany, 1780–1840: Some Mathematical and Philosophical Issues |journal=Historia Mathematica |volume=20 |number=3 |year=1993 |pages=265-284 |doi=10.1006/hmat.1993.1023}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Kenneth R. Manning |author-link=Kenneth Manning |title=The emergence of the Weierstrassian approach to complex analysis |journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences |year=1975 |volume=14 |pages=297–383 |jstor=41133437}}</ref> his treatise on analysis,{{sfn|Pfaff|1797a}} a paper{{sfn|Pfaff|1797b}} independently deriving [[Vandermonde's identity]] and proving [[Louis Saalschütz|Saalschütz's theorem]],<ref>{{cite journal |author=Jacques Dutka |title=The Early History of the Hypergeometric Function |journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences |year=1984 |volume=31 |number=1 |pages=15-34 |jstor=41133728}}</ref> and a paper{{sfn|Pfaff|1810}} solving for the largest ellipse that can be inscribed in a quadrilateral, a problem posed by Gauss.

Pfaff was the official doctoral advisor to [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]], who lived with him in Helmstedt in 1798, the one year of Gauss's residence at the university. Another notable acquaintance was [[Alexander von Humboldt]], whom Pfaff recommended to Göttingen.

While at Helmstedt, Pfaff was active outside of mathematics too, collaborating with [[Gottfried Gabriel Bredow]] on historical works. When the university's finances were in trouble, he wrote an essay{{sfn|Pfaff|1796}} defending it, preventing its closure. Pfaff served Helmstedt loyally, administering the university's pension fund for widows and refusing appointments at both Göttingen, for which he proposed Gauss, and [[University of Tartu|Dorpat]], for which he proposed his [[Johann Wilhelm Andreas Pfaff|brother]]; for his loyalty he was appointed [[Hofrat]] by the [[Charles William Ferdinand, Duke of Brunswick|Duke of Brunswick]].<ref name="dunnington"/>

On 8 November 1803, Pfaff married Sophie Wilhelmine Caroline Brand (b. 28 March 1784), his maternal cousin. 

When Helmstedt was abolished in 1810, Pfaff moved to the [[University of Halle]], where he remained for the rest of his career. In 1812, on the death of [[Georg Simon Klügel]], Pfaff became director of the observatory at Halle. While at Halle, he had several students, most notably [[August Möbius]].<ref name="dunnington">{{cite journal |title=Johann Friedrich Pfaff |author=G. Waldo Dunnington |author-link=G. Waldo Dunnington |journal=National Mathematics Magazine |volume=11 |number=6 |year=1937 |pages=263-266 |jstor=3028178}}</ref>

At Halle, Pfaff completed his most significant work{{sfn|Pfaff|1815}}, on [[partial differential equation]]s of the first order [[Pfaffian system]]s, as they are now called, which became part of the theory of [[differential form]]s. Despite a favorable review from Gauss on publication, it was not until a later assessment<ref>{{cite journal |author=C.G. Jacobi |title=Über Pfaff’s Methode, eine gewohnliche lineare Differentialgleichung zwischen 2 n Variabeln durch ein System von n Gleichungen zu integrieren |journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik |volume=2 |page=347 |language=de}}</ref> by [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi|Jacobi]] in 1827 that his work was widely recognized.<ref name="EB1911"/><ref name="samelson">{{cite journal |author=Hans Samelson |author-link=Hans Samelson |title=Differential Forms, the Early Days; or the Stories of Deahna's Theorem and of Volterra's Theorem |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=108 |number=6 |year=2001 |pages=522-530 |url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/2695706}}</ref><ref name="wussing"/>
Pfaff died 20 April 1825 in Halle of apoplexy.<ref name="dunnington"/>

Over his career, Pfaff joined several major academic societies, including the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]], the [[Göttingen Academy of Sciences]], the [[Prussian Academy of Sciences]], and the [[French Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="dunnington"/>

===Family===
Pfaff and his wife had two children, Carl Pfaff (b. 1 February 1805), who became a professor of philosophy and history at Halle, and Ludwig Pfaff (1811-1829).

Two of Pfaff's brothers also became notable academics: [[Johann Wilhelm Andreas Pfaff]] was a professor of [[Pure mathematics|pure]] and [[applied mathematics]], and [[Christoph Heinrich Pfaff]] was a professor of medicine, physics and chemistry.<ref name="EB1911"/>

[[File:Pfaff, Johann Friedrich – Commentatio de ortibus et occasibus siderum apud auctores classicos commemoratis, 1786 – BEIC 4641692.jpg|thumb|''Commentatio de ortibus et occasibus siderum apud auctores classicos commemoratis'', 1786]]

==Legacy==
{{Blockquote|text=They asked Laplace who, in his opinion, was the greatest mathematician of Germany. "It's Pfaff," he answered. - "I thought," the questioner replied, "that Gauss was superior to him." - "But," exclaimed Laplace, "you're asking me who is the greatest mathematician of Germany, and Gauss is the greatest mathematician of Europe.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hoefer |first1=Jean Christian Ferdinand |title=Nouvelle biographie universelle depuis les temps les plus reculés jusqu'a nos jours, avec les renseignements bibliographiques et l'indication des sources a consulter |date=1852 |publisher=Firmin Didot Freres |location=Paris |page=686|url=https://archive.org/details/nouvellebiograph19hoef|volume=19}}</ref>}}
